walkthroughs.body_html: Marine erosion operates via: 1) Hydraulic action: water and air compressed into joints exert 30+ tonnes/m2 pressure during storms; 2) Abrasion (corrasion): rock fragments thrown against the cliff act as a saw; 3) Attrition: clasts reduce one another to rounded shingle; 4) Solution (corrosion): weakly acidic seawater dissolves carbonate rock like chalk and limestone, important along the South Devon coast.

Sediment moves by four modes: traction (boulders rolled along bed), saltation (sand grains bouncing), suspension (silt held within turbulent flow), and solution (dissolved load). Longshore drift dominates lateral transport: prevailing waves approach obliquely (~30deg), swash carries sediment up the beach at that angle, backwash retreats vertically under gravity, producing zigzag movement and feeding spits like Spurn Head and Dawlish Warren.

England and Wales are divided into 11 sediment cells, each a near-closed system bounded by major headlands or estuaries. For example, Cell 2 stretches from Flamborough Head to The Wash. Sources: cliff erosion, rivers (~10% in UK), offshore. Transfers: longshore drift, tidal currents. Sinks: spits, bars, offshore bars, dunes. Shoreline Management Plans are designed at cell scale to ensure interventions in one location do not destabilise downdrift.

mcqs.q: Why do some rivers form deltas and others form estuaries?
options: Deltas form where rivers deposit sediment faster than the sea can remove it (calm seas, heavy load); estuaries form where tidal energy removes sediment (strong tides).
Deltas form in cold climates and estuaries in warm climates.
Deltas form on big rivers and estuaries on small ones.
